summary: On the road from Bethany, Jesus is hungry, finds a fig tree in full leaf but without fruit, and declares that no one will eat from it again.
key_insight: Mark adds the line that puzzles readers: “it was not the season for figs.” That is what made the tree stand out. It was in full leaf ahead of the season, advertising fruit it did not have. This is the one miracle in which Jesus pronounces a curse, and He spends it on a tree, as an acted warning.
story: Jesus had spent the night in Bethany. Early the next morning, as He was returning to the city, {Mt} He and the disciples came out from Bethany, and He was hungry. {Mk}
Seeing from a distance a fig tree in leaf, He went to see if perhaps He would find something on it. When He came to it, He found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. {Mk}
Jesus said to it, “Let no one eat fruit from you ever again.” And His disciples heard it. {Mk}
In Matthew’s account Jesus said, “Let no fruit grow on you ever again,” and immediately the fig tree withered away. {Mt}
differences: Matthew tells of the cursing after the clearing of the temple and finishes the story in one scene; Mark tells of the cursing before the clearing and of the withered tree the next morning.
Only Mark says Jesus saw the tree “from afar,” went to see “if perhaps He would find something on it,” and that “it was not the season for figs.”
Jesus’ words differ slightly: “Let no fruit grow on you ever again” (Matthew); “Let no one eat fruit from you ever again” (Mark).
Matthew says the tree withered “immediately”; Mark says only that “His disciples heard it,” and tells of the withering later.

fit.question: Matthew says the fig tree withered immediately and goes straight on to the disciples’ amazement. Mark says they found it withered the next morning. Which is it?

points.label: Withering began at once
points.text: Jesus’ word took effect when He spoke it. By the next morning the tree was “dried up from the roots” (Mark 11:20), dead through and through, which does not happen to a healthy tree overnight.

points.label: Matthew tells it as one story
points.text: Matthew often gathers related material together. He finishes the temple scene first (21:12–17), then tells the fig tree from start to finish (21:18–22). Mark keeps the day-by-day order and shows the disciples noticing the dead tree as they passed the next morning. Edersheim and McGarvey both read the accounts this way.

fit.note: Matthew tells the event by its meaning, Mark by its days. Both report the same curse and the same dead tree.
fit.short: The tree began to wither at Jesus’ word; the disciples noticed the next morning. Matthew tells the cursing and the discovery as one story.

scene.label: Figs in spring
scene.text: Fig trees in Israel put out their leaves in spring, around Passover, and with them small green knobs of early fruit; the main crop ripens in late summer. Edersheim notes that people on the road ate such unripe figs. A tree already in full leaf with nothing at all on it was likely barren.

scene.label: The prophets’ fig tree
scene.text: The prophets pictured God coming to Israel looking for fruit and finding none: “No grapes shall be on the vine, Nor figs on the fig tree, And the leaf shall fade” (Jeremiah 8:13; compare Micah 7:1). Prophets also acted out their warnings, as when Jeremiah smashed a clay flask before the elders (Jeremiah 19:10–11).

scene.label: A parable already told
scene.text: Months earlier, Jesus told of a man who looked for fruit on his fig tree three years in a row and found none. The vinedresser asked for one more year (Luke 13:6–9). Now, in Jerusalem’s last week, Jesus acts out the end of that story.

scene.label: Bethany to Jerusalem
scene.text: Through this week Jesus taught in the temple by day and spent the nights outside the city, at Bethany on the Mount of Olives (Mark 11:11, 19; Luke 21:37). Each morning the walk took Him back over the ridge toward the city.

witnesses.matthew: Tells the cursing and the withering together, right after the temple scene, so the fig tree stands as one complete picture: leaves, no fruit, judgment. He stresses that the tree withered “immediately” at Jesus’ word.
witnesses.mark: Splits the story around the temple scene and gives an onlooker’s details: the tree seen from far off, Jesus looking “if perhaps” He might find fruit, the note on the season, and “His disciples heard it.” The next morning Peter will remember.

seeing.reveals: Jesus truly hungered as a man, and He spoke with the authority of the Lord who comes to His people looking for fruit. His word that morning was a warning to Jerusalem before it was a judgment.
seeing.living: The tree’s problem was not a lack of leaves; leaves were all it had. Jesus is not impressed by the look of life. Ask Him where your faith has the leaves of religious activity without the fruit of a changed life.
seeing.ponder: If Jesus came looking for fruit in your life this morning, what would He find beneath the leaves?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus looks past the leaves for fruit, and fruitless religion stands under His judgment.
outline: A tree with leaves and no fruit (12–14)
A temple with business and no prayer (15–19)
preaching.watch_for: Mark builds a sandwich: the fig tree (11:12–14), the temple (11:15–19), the fig tree again (11:20–21). Each story explains the other. The barren tree pictures the busy temple, and the temple shows what the tree meant.
